summary: Describes experiments done in Japan by the P2P Network Experiment Council to show how an approach similar to ALTO can cut network traffic from peer-to-peer applications. It also gives guidance based on what was learned. It is informational.

eli5.summary: People tested whether file-sharing friends choosing nearby partners keeps the internet less jammed. They wrote down the results and what they learned.

questions: what experiments were done on alto in japan
what is alto application-layer traffic optimization
how does peer selection reduce network traffic
what did the japan p2p experiments show
subtitle: How Japan tested ALTO-like peer selection to reduce P2P traffic

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer file sharing applications create inefficient traffic patterns by choosing peers without regard to network topology, wasting bandwidth across ISP boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The P2P Network Experiment Council deployed hint servers that tell P2P applications which peers are topologically closer, allowing applications to select nearby peers instead of distant ones.
tldr.outcome: Experiments showed that hint servers reduced mean network distance by 10% and the 95th percentile by 5%, proving the ALTO concept could reduce inter-ISP traffic.

today: RFC 6875 documents experiments that were conducted from 2007 to 2008 and represents the historical work of the P2P Network Experiment Council. The insights informed the ALTO protocol, which has since matured as a standards track proposal. The document remains informational and unobsoleted.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
In the mid-2000s, peer-to-peer file sharing in Japan faced a crisis. P2P applications like BitTorrent were reshaping global internet traffic, but in Japan, unique applications such as Winny and Share dominated. These applications generated enormous traffic that flowed inefficiently across ISP borders, overloading backbone networks and Internet Exchanges. Yet reducing this traffic seemed impossible without either blocking P2P or having the fragmented applications coordinate with ISP infrastructure.

The Japanese Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications responded by forming the P2P Network Experiment Council in 2006, bringing together ISPs, P2P vendors, and content providers. Their goal was pragmatic: test whether topology-aware peer selection could reduce backbone traffic without requiring a monolithic architecture or breaking privacy.
sections.eli5: Peer-to-peer file sharing was clogging up Japan's internet in the 2000s. A government council decided to try teaching the apps to be smarter about choosing which other computers to download from.

sections.title: The Hint Server Architecture
sections.content:
Rather than impose a top-down mandate, the Council designed hint servers: a protocol-neutral way for ISPs to share topology information with P2P applications. When a P2P node starts, it registers its IP address with a hint server. The hint server looks up the node's geographic location and Autonomous System (AS) number using public BGP routing data and geography databases. It then calculates distances to other peers using two metrics: the number of AS hops (distance between ISPs) and the physical distance between prefectures. The hint server returns a ranked list of candidate peers, with closer peers listed first.

This approach preserves ISP privacy by using only publicly available information (BGP routes, GeoIP databases, AS numbers) and never disclosing internal network topology. Each P2P application can weigh the hint server's suggestions according to its own needs.
sections.eli5: A hint server is like a helpful sign that says: 'Hey, these three friends live on your block, these five are in the next city, and the rest are far away.' P2P apps can choose to follow the sign or ignore it.

sections.title: The Dummy Node Experiment
sections.content:
To measure the real-world impact of P2P applications on the network, the Council could not simply monitor every user's computer (too invasive). Instead, they deployed 60 dummy nodes across 40 different ISPs' access networks. Each dummy node was a Linux server running Windows XP in a virtual machine, with a P2P application running inside. Packets were captured at the Linux level to observe how the P2P application behaved and where it sent traffic.

By analyzing thousands of connections from these dummy nodes, the Council could see the actual traffic patterns: which peers each node connected to, how much data flowed across ISP boundaries, and whether topology information helped. The measurement methodology proved effective even though it could not capture every individual user.
sections.eli5: Instead of spying on millions of people, they put 60 fake computers on real internet connections and watched what happened when they ran P2P apps.

sections.title: Results and Key Findings
sections.content:
The initial experiments without hint servers showed that P2P applications were selecting peers essentially at random: only 22% to 29% chose peers in the same ISP. When the hint server was introduced, the distance to peers decreased measurably. The mean distance decreased by 10%, and more significantly, the 95th percentile (longest distance) dropped by 5%, showing that even the worst-case peers became closer.

The Council also discovered that different P2P topologies (tree-based versus mesh-based) responded differently to hints. Tree-based P2P applications weighted the hints heavily and achieved better results, while mesh-based applications treated hints as one factor among many. The varying responsiveness showed that helping applications requires understanding their architecture.
sections.eli5: When the hint server was turned on, P2P apps started picking peers about 10% closer on average, and the farthest peers got much closer too.

sections.title: Lessons for ALTO and Hierarchical Control
sections.content:
Based on their experiments, the Council proposed two important additions to ALTO (Application-Layer Traffic Optimization). First, they recommended hierarchical ALTO servers that could operate at multiple granularities: coarse-grained servers for inter-ISP traffic selection, and fine-grained servers for peer selection within an ISP. This hierarchy lets each ISP disclose only the minimum information needed at each level. Second, they found that generic measurement mechanisms are critical, since each P2P application measures its own performance differently, making it hard to compare results. Standardizing measurement would help the ALTO ecosystem mature.

The Council's bottom-up, pragmatic approach contrasted with top-down proposals like P4P, proving that industry-driven experiments could yield actionable insights for protocol design.
sections.eli5: The experiment taught that ALTO servers should work in layers (ask 'what ISP' first, then 'what peer'), and everyone needs to measure things the same way to know if it's working.
